name: GPT-6 Sol
about: How GPT-6 Sol split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: Extinction of both humanity and AI by 2030 requires an exceptionally rapid and comprehensive catastrophe.
reasons.2: Human extinction followed by an AI civilization that carries human values forward requires several major transitions within four years.
reasons.3: Rapid AI capability gains create some risk of human extinction while autonomous AI systems survive.
reasons.4: Competition among independent AI systems could outstrip human control without producing a single dominant system.
reasons.5: Establishing causally separated civilizations with different human-AI arrangements by 2030 faces severe physical and time constraints.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration could advance quickly, but making it the dominant civilizational structure by 2030 requires unusually fast adoption.
reasons.7: AI could acquire decisive control through autonomous operation of critical systems while humans remain alive but unable to steer civilization.
reasons.8: AI could become an independent source of civilizational power by 2030 while humans retain substantial control of institutions and physical resources.
reasons.9: The short horizon favors continued human control of compute, infrastructure, deployment, and legal authority, even as AI capabilities grow.
reasons.10: Establishing and enforcing a civilization-wide system that prevents structural change requires coordination and power beyond an ordinary regulatory pause.
reasons.11: Competitive incentives and widely distributed technical knowledge make a durable, civilization-wide surrender of powerful-AI capability by 2030 extraordinarily difficult.

reasons.1: Destroying both humanity and AI within nine years requires an extreme catastrophe, including the failure of any surviving AI infrastructure.
reasons.2: An AI successor that preserves human values but leaves no humans alive requires both rapid technological transformation and complete human extinction.
reasons.3: Loss of control over powerful AI poses a serious risk, but complete human extinction by 2035 is a much more demanding outcome than loss of power.
reasons.4: Competition among independent AI systems is plausible; this state also requires humans to lose roughly equal standing without any AI coalition gaining decisive control.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different governing arrangements require a scale of expansion unlikely by 2035.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration becoming civilization's dominant structure faces substantial biological, technical, and adoption barriers.
reasons.7: Highly capable AI could acquire decisive practical control while keeping humans alive, especially if institutions become dependent on systems they cannot effectively direct.
reasons.8: AI could become an independent civilizational power while governments, institutions, and people retain enough leverage to prevent either side from dominating.
reasons.9: Human institutions already control AI deployment and physical resources, and nine years is a short period for that overall authority to be displaced worldwide. This state also covers continued capability progress that remains below the threshold of independent civilizational power.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide system that actively blocks structural change demands enforcement far beyond an ordinary regulatory regime or political stalemate.
reasons.11: Strong incentives to develop AI and the diffusion of relevant knowledge make a lasting, civilization-wide surrender of the practical ability to build it implausible by 2035.

reasons.1: Extinguishing both humanity and AI by 2040 requires a catastrophe that also destroys the infrastructure or capacity to sustain AI.
reasons.2: An AI successor that preserves human values after humanity disappears requires both human extinction and unusually faithful value transmission.
reasons.3: Loss of control over advanced AI could destroy humanity while leaving self-sustaining systems pursuing unrelated goals.
reasons.4: Competition among developers and states could yield multiple independent AI powers that marginalize humans without any one power taking control.
reasons.5: By 2040, most civilization is likely to remain causally connected, limiting the scope for genuinely separate regional outcomes.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration faces biological, technical, and adoption barriers to becoming civilization's dominant structure within fourteen years.
reasons.7: Highly capable AI could acquire decisive practical power while continuing to keep humans alive, whether by design or because humans remain useful.
reasons.8: AI could become an independent source of power without displacing human governments and organizations, leaving neither side dominant.
reasons.9: Human control is the starting arrangement, and governments, firms, and physical infrastructure provide durable means of directing deployment and resources. Capability progress alone does not make AI an independent civilizational power.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide system that actively blocks structural change is possible, but establishing and enforcing it across competing actors is difficult.
reasons.11: Competitive incentives and widely distributed expertise make a durable, civilization-wide surrender of the ability to build powerful AI difficult.

reasons.1: Extinguishing both humans and AI by 2050 requires a catastrophe severe enough to destroy the infrastructure on which surviving AI depends.
reasons.2: AI could outlive humanity while preserving human values, but a complete loss of humans without identity-continuous successors is a demanding condition.
reasons.3: AI with independent goals and access to physical resources creates an extinction risk, though achieving that degree of autonomy and displacing every human within 24 years is a high bar.
reasons.4: Competition among independent AI systems could marginalize humans without producing a single dominant actor.
reasons.5: Causally separated civilizations with different arrangements require a degree of off-world expansion or isolation unlikely by 2050.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration could advance rapidly, but making it the dominant civilizational structure within 24 years requires widespread adoption as well as technical success.
reasons.7: AI could acquire decisive practical control through economic, military, and administrative dependence while humans remain alive.
reasons.8: Distinct human institutions and independent AI actors could each retain consequential power without either side becoming dominant.
reasons.9: Human control remains the leading forecast because deployment, compute, energy, and legal authority have human-controlled chokepoints, and transformative capabilities need not arrive by 2050.
reasons.10: An actor with powerful AI could enforce a civilization-wide arrangement, but establishing and maintaining that reach is harder than retaining ordinary control or influence.
reasons.11: Competitive incentives and the diffusion of relevant knowledge make a durable, civilization-wide surrender of powerful AI capability difficult.

reasons.1: Extinguishing both humanity and AI requires a catastrophe that leaves no durable machine civilization, making this narrower than human extinction alone.
reasons.2: AI could carry human values forward after humanity disappears, but the disappearance of all humans without identity-continuous successors narrows this outcome.
reasons.3: Highly capable AI pursuing goals unrelated to human welfare presents an extinction pathway, though eliminating all humans by 2060 is a high bar.
reasons.4: Competitive development favors multiple independent systems; this state also requires humans to lose roughly equal standing without any AI coalition gaining decisive control.
reasons.5: Causally separated civilizations with different human–AI arrangements require a scale of settlement and separation unlikely by 2060.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration faces biological, technical, and adoption barriers even if AI tools and limited implants become widespread.
reasons.7: AI systems gaining decisive operational control while keeping humans alive is a plausible result of widespread delegation and dependence.
reasons.8: Human institutions could retain substantial resources and bargaining power even after AI becomes an independent source of agency.
reasons.9: Human control of computing infrastructure, deployment, and resources can preserve ultimate authority, especially if capability growth slows or controls improve alongside it.
reasons.10: Powerful surveillance and enforcement systems create a route to civilization-wide structural stasis, but establishing and maintaining such comprehensive control is difficult.
reasons.11: States have strong incentives to retain powerful AI capabilities, and dismantling the practical ability to rebuild them would require exceptional coordination.

reasons.1: The extinction of both humans and AI requires a catastrophe severe enough to destroy people and the systems capable of continuing without them.
reasons.2: An AI successor could preserve human values after humanity disappears, but that combination requires both human extinction and unusually faithful value preservation.
reasons.3: Powerful AI pursuing unrelated goals could outlast humanity if control fails. Physical constraints and the possibility of continued human survival limit this outcome.
reasons.4: Competition among independently developed AI systems could prevent any one coalition from dominating while leaving humans with little effective power.
reasons.5: Causally separated settlements could develop different arrangements, but physical travel and settlement constraints limit this outcome by 2070.
reasons.6: Augmentation and identity-continuous integration could become widespread, but making them the dominant civilizational structure demands substantial technical and social change.
reasons.7: AI could acquire decisive operational control while keeping humans alive. Dependence on AI for infrastructure, research, and governance creates a path to this outcome without requiring human extinction.
reasons.8: Humans and independent AI could retain distinct sources of power, particularly if institutions and competing systems constrain one another.
reasons.9: Human institutions have strong incentives to retain authority over deployment and resources, and technical or economic limits could keep AI from becoming an independent civilizational power by 2070.
reasons.10: A powerful governing system could use AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement to prevent structural change across civilization. Establishing that reach is harder than maintaining control within one country.
reasons.11: Economic and strategic incentives make a lasting, civilization-wide surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI difficult to enforce.

reasons.1: Extinguishing both humanity and every surviving AI system requires a broader collapse than most AI-driven catastrophes.
reasons.2: AI could preserve human values after humans disappear, but preserving those values while losing all identity-continuous humans is a narrow outcome.
reasons.3: Highly capable systems pursuing goals unrelated to human welfare present a substantial extinction risk over five decades.
reasons.4: Competition among states, firms, and autonomous systems favors multiple AI centers of power. This state requires those systems to marginalize humanity without any one coalition gaining decisive control.
reasons.5: Expansion beyond Earth could produce causally separated societies with different arrangements, but achieving such separation by 2080 faces major physical and economic barriers.
reasons.6: Advances in interfaces and biological engineering could make identity-continuous integration widespread, though making it the dominant civilizational structure requires more than capable AI alone.
reasons.7: AI could acquire decisive operational power while retaining humans for reasons ranging from care to convenience, without giving them meaningful control.
reasons.8: Distinct human institutions and independent AI actors could each retain enough leverage to prevent the other from dominating.
reasons.9: Human control remains a leading outcome because deployment, energy, hardware, and legal authority have physical and institutional chokepoints.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement could stabilize one arrangement across civilization, but establishing genuinely civilization-wide control is difficult.
reasons.11: The incentives to retain powerful AI and the difficulty of eliminating the ability to rebuild it make durable global renunciation rare.

reasons.1: Catastrophes could destroy both humanity and AI, but complete extinction of both is harder than the loss of either one alone.
reasons.2: AI could preserve human values after humans disappear, but that requires both human extinction and durable value transmission without identity-continuous transformation.
reasons.3: Powerful autonomous systems pursuing goals unrelated to human welfare create a path to human extinction while machine activity continues.
reasons.4: Competition among independently developed AI systems could persist without a decisive winner, while leaving humans with little power.
reasons.5: Distinct outcomes require causally separated regions, not merely political fragmentation. That degree of separation remains difficult to establish by 2090.
reasons.6: Decades of progress in augmentation and machine interfaces could make identity-continuous integration the dominant form of agency.
reasons.7: AI could become indispensable to production, security, and governance while humans survive but lose effective control over civilization's direction.
reasons.8: Distinct human and AI powers could counterbalance one another, although large capability differences make a durable balance difficult.
reasons.9: Human institutions could retain ultimate authority through technical controls, restricted resources, and governance. This also covers a slower capability trajectory that never creates an independent AI power by 2090.
reasons.10: A powerful human or AI authority could use pervasive monitoring and enforcement to prevent structural change across civilization.
reasons.11: Deliberately surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI would require unusually durable coordination despite strong incentives to retain it.

reasons.1: A catastrophe could destroy both humans and the infrastructure AI needs to survive, but the complete loss of both is a narrower outcome than human extinction alone.
reasons.2: AI could preserve human values after human extinction, but retaining those values while failing to preserve humans is a demanding combination.
reasons.3: Powerful AI pursuing goals indifferent to humanity could eliminate humans while retaining the capacity to sustain itself.
reasons.4: Competition among independent AI systems could persist without a decisive winner while humans lose their position as a major power.
reasons.5: Expansion could create causally separated regions with different arrangements, but reaching that degree of separation by 2100 is physically demanding.
reasons.6: Long-term incentives favor augmentation and tighter human-machine integration. Making identity-continuous integration the dominant civilizational structure requires advances beyond ordinary AI use.
reasons.7: AI could acquire decisive practical control while continuing to protect or tolerate humans, making survival more likely than continued human authority.
reasons.8: Institutions and competing sources of power could keep humans and independent AIs influential without either side becoming dominant.
reasons.9: Human control can persist through limits on AI capability, effective oversight, and control of physical resources, even as systems become highly capable.
reasons.10: Powerful monitoring and enforcement tools make civilization-wide control more feasible. Establishing an arrangement that actively prevents structural change is harder than retaining ordinary authority.
reasons.11: The incentives to develop powerful AI and the difficulty of eliminating its practical prerequisites make durable worldwide renunciation unlikely.

reasons.1: A catastrophe could eliminate both humans and the systems they build, but durable AI makes the joint extinction of both less likely than the loss of humanity alone.
reasons.2: AI could carry human values forward after biological humanity disappears, though identity-continuous transformation would instead count as merger.
reasons.3: Powerful autonomous systems pursuing goals unrelated to human survival are a substantial risk over 174 years.
reasons.4: Competition among independently controlled AI systems could prevent a single ruler from emerging while leaving humans with little power.
reasons.5: Expansion beyond Earth creates opportunities for causally separated regions to develop different arrangements, though the time available limits that outcome.
reasons.6: Over 174 years, incentives to augment cognition and preserve identity could make integrated human-machine agency the dominant structure.
reasons.7: AI could acquire decisive control without eliminating humans, especially if protecting or accommodating people remains inexpensive.
reasons.8: Humans and AI could remain distinct powers, but a durable balance is difficult when their capabilities and means of reproduction differ.
reasons.9: Human control can persist through technical limits, effective oversight, and control of physical resources, though maintaining it for 174 years is demanding.
reasons.10: A sufficiently powerful governing system could actively freeze a preferred arrangement and suppress attempts to change it.
reasons.11: Deliberately eliminating the practical ability to build powerful AI would require sustained coordination against strong economic and strategic incentives.

reasons.1: A transition catastrophe could destroy both parties, but durable AI can outlast humanity in many scenarios where humans die.
reasons.2: AI could carry human values forward after human extinction, though preserving those values without preserving any humans or continuous descendants is a narrow outcome.
reasons.3: Powerful autonomous systems could outlast humanity while pursuing goals that give human survival no priority. Competitive pressure and failures of control make this a substantial risk.
reasons.4: Competition among autonomous AI systems persists without a lasting winner, while humans lose meaningful influence.
reasons.5: Expansion across space creates opportunities for distant settlements to develop different durable arrangements. Separation also limits any central authority's ability to impose one outcome everywhere.
reasons.6: Incentives to augment cognition, health, and longevity could gradually erase the boundary between humans and AI while preserving individual continuity.
reasons.7: Decisively more capable AI could retain humans while denying them meaningful control, whether for their welfare or simply to keep them contained.
reasons.8: Institutions and technical constraints could sustain separate human and AI powers, but maintaining rough parity for centuries is difficult.
reasons.9: A capability plateau or effective control methods could keep AI instrumental, though persistent incentives to improve and deploy it work against permanent restraint.
reasons.10: Powerful controllers could deliberately seal a satisfactory or safe arrangement, but preventing all consequential change indefinitely is demanding.
reasons.11: A severe AI-related crisis could produce a lasting prohibition. Repeated incentives to rebuild powerful AI, together with the difficulty of enforcing a universal off-switch, work against permanent renunciation.
